verdict.reasoning: Patient reports upper lip swelling and difficulty breathing after prawn soup: "there is like a swelling on my, on my upper lip" and "I feel like I can't breathe that well right now" after ordering "a prawn soup".
Onset and location described: swelling started "in the corner sort of on the left first" and she says it developed in about "half an hour" with sensation "really pumping blood" and getting bigger.

She reports dizziness and breathing difficulty that may involve the chest: "I feel a little dizzy right now" and "I don't know if it's the chest it just generally feels a little difficult, but yeah it might be, I'm not sure."

She describes a similar episode about a year ago after late-night Chinese/curry with swelling and breathing problems: "maybe, I remember like a year ago" ... "late night kinda Chinese place" ... "I was quite swollen up and had also I, felt really bad and quite difficult breathing."
She clearly states a history of asthma: "I generally have asthma so, I took I, I take, ohh what's it called? Salbutamol inhalers?" and repeats "I generally have asthma."

Medication history: she uses Salbutamol and denies other inhalers: "Salbutamol inhalers?" ... "Yeah, so I do take that regularly" and to question about other/brown inhalers: "Ohh I, no I don't think so, no."

Childhood severe peanut reaction with hospital care and injection is described: "I have a peanut allergy as well, like always had it" and doctor asks if she ever needed an injection or hospital; she answers "When I was a kid I think I remember my mom told me about it" and later confirms hospital: "Yeah is that well I was like six or something" in context of severe allergic reaction.

Current episode clearly linked to prawn soup: "I ordered a prawn soup" and symptoms started afterward; doctor concludes it "sounds like you could be going into ... an anaphylactic reaction" based on this history, making prawn/shellfish the suspected trigger.

Doctor explicitly suspects anaphylaxis with these features: "sounds like you could be going into ... an anaphylactic reaction" after prawn soup; patient has acute upper lip swelling ("swelling on my upper lip"), shortness of breath ("I feel like I can't breathe that well"), possible chest tightness ("I don't know if it's the chest"), dizziness ("I feel a little dizzy right now"), all beginning about "half an hour" after ingestion.

History of peanut anaphylaxis and asthma are both present: she has "peanut allergy" with prior severe reaction requiring hospital and injection in childhood, and states "I generally have asthma" and uses Salbutamol.

Doctor initiates emergency response: "I think we need to call an ambulance" and instructs mum to call 999 for suspected anaphylaxis: "say that your there is a suspected anaphylactic reaction and they need to come straight away."

Doctor advises antihistamine use while waiting: "Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around, in the interim, while we're waiting" and later "so straight away take the antihistamines in the meantime all right."
Doctor explicitly instructs her not to be alone until EMS arrives: "make sure that person's with you till the ambulance comes."

Post-hospital follow-up and epinephrine-type injection are mentioned: "after you come out from the hospital do give us a ring back we might need to sort you out, um, with your injections and things like that" in the context of anaphylaxis management.
